title: ulimit doesn't cap memory on macOS: stop a job before it swaps
summary: macOS lacks memory capping mechanisms like Linux's ulimit or cgroups, causing memory-heavy jobs to swap instead of failing. The article provides monitoring commands (sysctl) and introduces stageload, a library that guards against excessive memory use by monitoring swap growth and terminating processes before system slowdown.
content:
On Linux a job's memory can be capped with ulimit -v, systemd-run -p MemoryMax= or a cgroup, and a job that grows too big fails on its own instead of taking the machine down. macOS has no systemd and no cgroups, and ulimit refuses. This is macOS 26.5.2:
$ /bin/bash -c 'ulimit -v 1048576'
/bin/bash: line 0: ulimit: virtual memory: cannot modify limit: Invalid argument
$ /bin/bash -c 'ulimit -m 1048576'
/bin/bash: line 0: ulimit: max memory size: cannot modify limit: Invalid argument

resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_DATA, ...) in Python raises ValueError, and in the shell where ulimit -m had failed, a script went on to allocate and touch 3 GiB. What macOS does instead is compress memory and write it to swap. A model that doesn't fit doesn't fail: it slows down, and so does everything else on the Mac.
So the questions worth asking change: is there room before a job starts, and is swap growing while it runs?
sysctl vm.swapusage             # compare "used" before and after a run
sysctl kern.memorystatus_level  # system-wide free memory, in percent

The process footprint, the number Activity Monitor shows, doesn't count pages that are already in swap. In one run of Qwen-Image-2.1 with diffusers' model CPU offload on my 48 GB M5 Pro, the footprint never went above 18.5 GB while swap grew by 9.6 GB. A chart of the footprint alone would have called that run a fit.
stageload, a small library I wrote for loading models one stage at a time, ships a guard for this (pip install stageload):
stageload guard --wait-free 40 --swap-budget 8G -- python generate.py

It waits until kern.memorystatus_level is at least 40 %, then starts the command. If swap grows more than 8 GB over what was in use at the start, or free memory stays under 10 % for two samples, it sends SIGTERM to the command's process group and, five seconds later, SIGKILL to whatever is left. It needs no root, and the command and its process group are the only processes it ever stops. Exit code 3 means the guard stopp

title: Balancing AI Integration and Manual Coding: Addressing Frustration in Programming Practices
summary: As AI tools automate coding tasks, experienced developers face frustration over skill atrophy and loss of craftsmanship. The article examines the tension between efficiency-driven AI adoption and the intrinsic value of hands-on problem-solving, arguing that homogenized AI solutions risk stifling innovation and diverse approaches.
content:
Introduction: The Rise of AI in Programming


The programming landscape is undergoing a seismic shift as AI tools increasingly permeate workflows, automating tasks like code generation, debugging, and optimization. This integration, driven by demands for faster development cycles and cost efficiency, is reshaping the industry. However, this technological advancement is not without its friction. For programmers like the poster, who have spent 15 years honing their craft, the rise of AI represents a threat to the intrinsic values that define their profession: craftsmanship, creativity, and the joy of hands-on problem-solving.
The integration of AI tools is altering the traditional coding process by abstracting away manual tasks. For instance, AI-powered code generation can produce functional code in seconds, but this efficiency comes at a cost. The causal chain is clear: impact of AI adoption -> internal process of skill atrophy -> observable effect of declining foundational skills. As developers rely more on AI, their ability to debug complex issues or optimize code manually may atrophy, leading to a dependency on automated solutions. This is not merely a theoretical risk; it’s a mechanism of deformation in the skill set of programmers, where the very muscles of their craft weaken from underuse.
The poster’s frustration is rooted in a deeper philosophical conflict: the tension between efficiency-driven adoption of AI and the intrinsic value of manual coding. For them, programming is not just a job but a labor of love, driven by curiosity and the enjoyment of the process. AI tools, while powerful, threaten to homogenize the coding experience, replacing unique problem-solving approaches with standardized solutions. This homogenization is not just a loss of creativity but a risk of stifling innovation, as diverse perspectives are squeezed out by the dominance of AI-generated code.

title: How I Hunted Down 23 N+1 Queries in a Rails App With Claude Code
summary: A developer paired with Claude Code to find and fix 23 N+1 queries in a legacy Rails app, reducing p95 response time from 1.4s to under 400ms through systematic testing. The breakthrough was requiring failing tests before implementing each fix, which prevented a first-pass approach that initially made endpoints slower.
content:
TL;DR


Our Rails app's p95 response time had crept from 280 ms to 1.4 s over a year, and nobody could say why. I paired with Claude Code for four days, found 23 N+1 queries, fixed 19 of them, and got p95 back under 400 ms. The real win wasn't the fixes, though: it was making Claude prove every N+1 with a failing test before touching the code, because the first "fix everything with includes" pass made two endpoints slower.
Here's the setup: a seven-year-old Rails monolith (Rails 7.1, Ruby 3.3, PostgreSQL 16), about 140 models, a B2B dashboard that customers live in all day. Nothing was on fire. It was just... slow. The kind of slow where support tickets say "the app feels sluggish" and nobody can reproduce anything specific.
When I pulled APM data, the pattern was obvious in hindsight:
p95 on the dashboard endpoint: 1.4 s (was ~280 ms a year earlier)
Average SQL queries per request on the top 10 endpoints: 187
Worst single request I could find: 2,341 queries to render one page
Nobody had written a "bad" query. Every one of those queries was a perfectly reasonable SELECT ... WHERE id = $1. The problem was that they ran inside loops, inside partials, inside serializers, inside helper methods that called other helper methods. Classic N+1, spread across hundreds of files.
I'd tried fixing this by hand twice before. Both times I got through three or four endpoints, got pulled onto feature work, and the gains evaporated as new code reintroduced the same patterns. This time I wanted two things:
Find all of them, not just the ones I happened to notice.
Make sure they stay fixed.
That second goal turned out to be the one that mattered.
My first instinct was to open Claude Code and say "find N+1 queries in this app." I did exactly that, and it came back with a list of 60+ "suspicious" associations based on reading the code. Most were false positives: associations that looked like they'd loop, but were only ever called on a single record.
Static reading isn't enough for N+1s.

title: My Triton Kernel Ties bitsandbytes — and Both Lose to Math
summary: This technical article details implementing a fused W4A16 GEMV kernel in Triton for batch-1 LLM decoding, measuring performance against RTX 3060 hardware roofline limits. Three kernel versions were tested and correctness-verified against PyTorch references; the fused version proved fastest despite theoretical advantages of a tuned variant.
content:
A fused W4A16 GEMV for batch-1 decoding, measured against the RTX 3060 roofline.

Scope note: one RTX 3060 12GB, batch-1 greedy decoding, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. This is a learning kernel, stated as such — the point is understanding, not beating Marlin.
Batch-1 decoding is memory-bandwidth bound: each token reads every weight byte once. So the ceiling is bandwidth divided by the bytes read per token (weights plus a 2,048-token KV-cache read) — worked out before any code.
Measured (torch copy benchmark, not the spec sheet): 323.9 GB/s (spec: 360).

Two details worth knowing: the tied 151,936-token embedding is ~15% of Qwen's weights, and ORCH's matrices are so small that launch overhead may dominate — tested below.
Three versions, all correctness-tested against a PyTorch reference on the models' real matrix shapes before any number was reported:
v1 (dequantise-then-matmul): materialise fp16, then torch matmul. Shows the cost of the extra memory pass — 3–7× slower than v2.
v2 (fused): one kernel, dequantise on the fly, no materialisation.
v3 (split-K + tuned): autotuned tiles, split-K parallelism for large matrices.
Per-shape microbenchmarks (in the repo) hold one more surprise: v3 is not faster than v2 on any of the five shapes I measured (v2 is 1.0–1.4× faster), yet end-to-end decoding uses v3. The fused kernel itself is up to 5.5× faster than a pre-dequantised reference on the wide MLP-gate shape; swapping v2 into the decode loop is the obvious next experiment.
Two bugs found along the way, both load-bearing:
Missing +8 zero-point in packing — every positive weight destroyed. Caught by review before first GPU run.

title: Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK v2: The Enterprise Automation Engine for Entra ID
summary: After legacy PowerShell modules were deprecated, enterprise teams migrated to Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK v2, which requires optimization to avoid performance and rate-limiting issues. The article covers certificate-based authentication for CI/CD and micro-module imports to reduce startup latency by 15–25 seconds, with reference implementations for automated workflows.
content:
The deprecation of legacy PowerShell modules (AzureAD, AzureADPreview, and MSOnline) forced identity and cloud security teams worldwide to migrate their entire automation stack to the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK v2.
However, many engineers discovered that naive scripts written for Graph SDK v2 suffered from sluggish performance, rate-limiting HTTP 429 throttling errors, and oversized authentication token scopes.
In this enterprise engineering guide, we break down how to architect robust, high-performance identity automation engines using Microsoft Graph SDK v2, including:
App-Only certificate authentication (Zero manual interactive prompts in CI/CD).
Slashing Module Load Time: Avoid Import-Module Microsoft.Graph
The monolithic Microsoft.Graph module bundles dozens of sub-modules encompassing thousands of cmdlets. Importing the full module adds 15–25 seconds of startup latency to every Azure Automation runbook or GitHub Actions workflow.
Instead, import only the precise micro-modules your runbook requires:
powershell
Import-Module Microsoft.Graph.Authentication
Unattended Enterprise Authentication via Certificate
Hardcoded client secrets create credential leakage risks and expire unpredictably. Enterprise automation must leverage certificate-based authentication against Microsoft Entra ID App Registrations:
powershell

    -ClientId $ClientId

    -CertificateThumbprint $CertificateThumbprint
Production Script: Automated Zero Trust Leaver Offboarding Runbook
When an employee departs, deprovisioning must be atomic across sessions, credentials, group memberships, and privileged roles:
powershell
[CmdletBinding()]
Open-Source Repositories & Full Guide
All automation scripts and production cmdlets from this article are maintained open-source on GitHub:
📦 Shivi7566/graph-api-toolkit

content:
Choosing an artifact repository is less about who has the longest feature list, and more about which deployment model fits your team size, stack, compliance needs, and budget. For self-hosted setups, Sonatype Nexus and JFrog Artifactory are the pair most often compared. If you are already deeply tied to a cloud or code host, GitHub Packages or Google Artifact Registry is usually less work. Teams that want open-source control and room to extend can also look at self-hosted options such as AngusRepo.
This article helps you filter among those categories. If you have already narrowed to Nexus, Artifactory, and AngusRepo, read 2026 private artifact repository selection: Nexus, Artifactory, AngusRepo deep comparison for a finer product-level comparison of formats, security, storage, and operations.

title: Ethereum RPC Providers for Developers: NOWNodes, Alchemy, Infura, QuickNode, GetBlock, and Chainstack
summary: Six Ethereum RPC providers (NOWNodes, Alchemy, Infura, QuickNode, GetBlock, Chainstack) abstract away node operation for multi-chain wallet backends via a standardized JSON-RPC interface. The article explains connection methods and compares providers by chain coverage, traffic handling, and cost; switching typically requires only a URL change.
content:
Say you're building a multi-chain wallet backend. It needs Ethereum, a couple of L2s, and — because your users hold it — Bitcoin. You do not want to sync and babysit a node for each chain. So you reach for an Ethereum RPC provider: a service that runs the node and hands you a URL to send JSON-RPC calls to.
Six names come up for that job: NOWNodes, Alchemy, Infura, QuickNode, GetBlock, and Chainstack. They all speak the same protocol, so the hard part isn't writing the code — it's picking the one that fits your chains, your traffic, and your bill. This post covers both: how to connect, and how to choose.
TL;DR
The rest of this is the reasoning and the code behind that list.
How an RPC Provider Fits Into Your App
RPC stands for remote procedure call: you ask a remote server to run a function and return the result. eth_getBalance, eth_call, eth_sendRawTransaction — each is a request your app fires at a node over HTTPS or WebSocket. Ethereum clients expose a standard method set, documented in Ethereum.org's JSON-RPC reference.
A provider runs that node behind an authenticated URL and keeps the client patched and the hardware scaled. Because the method set is standardized, the same request works whether it hits a self-hosted Geth node or a managed endpoint — which is why switching providers later is usually a URL change, not a rewrite.
The raw version, with curl:
bash
curl -X POST https://eth.nownodes.io \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "api-key: YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"eth_getBalance","params":["0xd8dA6BF26964aF9D7eEd9e03E53415D37aA96045","latest"]}'

Connecting With ethers.js
You rarely hand-roll JSON-RPC in production — you point a library at the endpoint. The only provider-specific part is authentication; here NOWNodes takes the key in an api-key header.
ethers.js (v6):
js
const req = new ethers.FetchRequest("https://eth.nownodes.io");
const provider = new ethers.JsonRpcProvider(req);
const balance = await provider.getBal

title: Agentic development: perché il frontend sta cambiando più in fretta dell’infrastruttura
summary: Agentic AI development is changing frontend work faster than underlying infrastructure can adapt, enabling automation of manual tasks like scaffolding and boilerplate. The rise of self-hosted models offers teams deeper control over data and integration, but existing CI/CD and audit systems weren't designed for AI agents.
content:
Dai modelli self-hosted agli agenti che scrivono codice: opportunità, limiti e responsabilità in un nuovo paradigma di sviluppo.
Negli ultimi anni abbiamo visto l’AI passare da “supporto” a “forza operativa”: non solo suggerisce una riga di codice, ma può esplorare un repository, proporre refactor, creare componenti, aggiornare dipendenze, generare test e aprire pull request. In pratica, stiamo entrando in un’era in cui chiunque può costruire qualcosa — e dove la distanza tra idea e prototipo si accorcia drasticamente.
Questo cambiamento, però, non è solo tecnologico: è un cambio di paradigma. Perché mentre gli agenti diventano più capaci, l’infrastruttura (tecnica e organizzativa) con cui sviluppiamo non è stata progettata per loro.
Siamo in un periodo in cui la sensazione diffusa è: com’è possibile che tutto stia cambiando così in fretta?.
Modelli sempre più grandi e competenti ampliano ciò che è realizzabile.
Tooling sempre più accessibile riduce la barriera d’ingresso.
L’effetto combinato è una democratizzazione della produzione software.
Per il frontend questo significa che molte attività “manuali” (impalcature di progetto, boilerplate, conversioni tra formati, scaffolding di componenti, wiring di API) sono ormai candidati naturali all’automazione.
Un aspetto spesso sottovalutato è la crescita di soluzioni self-hosted e di modelli eseguibili in locale.
In termini pratici, per aziende e team frontend questo apre un “secondo binario”:
Maggiore controllo su dati e proprietà intellettuale.
Integrazioni più profonde con repository e ambienti interni.
Riduzione della dipendenza da servizi esterni per task sensibili.
Questa direzione abilita scenari in cui l’AI non è un servizio remoto “a cui chiedere”, ma una capacità interna, disponibile vicino al codice e ai processi.
Qui emerge la frizione principale: l’ecosistema con cui lavoriamo (pipeline, permessi, CI/CD, ambienti di esecuzione, metriche, audit) è stato pensato per sviluppatori umani e automazioni tradizionali

title: Girora: Plan Trips with AI and Find People to Travel With
summary: Girora is a travel companion app that uses locally-run AI to help users plan trips, generate itineraries, and find others with similar travel interests to join their journeys, solving the fragmentation of travel planning across multiple apps.
content:
My submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 1: Touch Grass.
I built Girora, a travel companion app that helps people plan trips, share their travel plans, and find others who might want to join them.
The idea came from a simple problem: planning a trip involves a lot of small decisions. You have to choose a destination, figure out the dates and budget, plan what to do, and sometimes find people who are interested in going with you. These things can end up scattered across different apps, websites, and conversations.
I wanted to bring the main parts of this process together in one place.
Girora is built around three things: planning a trip, sharing it with others, and discovering trips to join.
Sometimes you know you want to travel, but you don't know where to start with the planning. You might have a destination in mind, a limited budget, or only a few days available.
Girora includes an AI itinerary-generation feature that helps turn travel preferences into a suggested plan. The idea is to give users a starting point instead of making them plan every detail from scratch.
For the AI part, I used Gemma 3 1B through Ollama, running locally on my computer. This gave me a way to experiment with an open-weight model and connect its generated output to the application.
Girora also lets users create trips with details such as the destination, dates, and budget.
The idea is that a trip shouldn't have to remain a private plan. Once created, it can be shared so other people can discover it and see whether it interests them.
This is the community part of the project.
Users can browse trips and express interest in joining one by sending a join request. Instead of everyone having to plan separately, Girora is intended to make it easier for people with similar travel interests to connect around a trip.
The current version demonstrates the trip discovery and join-request flows, but it doesn't yet have a shared backend. Trip data and join requests are stored

title: # I Built a .gitignore Generator Because Setting Up a Project Should Be Simpler
summary: DotGitIgnore.com is a free generator that creates technology-appropriate .gitignore files, eliminating the need to manually hunt templates or remember exclusion rules for different tech stacks and frameworks.
content:
Every developer has probably done this at some point.
You create a new project, initialize Git, and then realize you still need to create a .gitignore file.
If you're working with a familiar stack, you probably know which files and directories to exclude. But when you're starting a new project, switching technologies, or working with an unfamiliar tool, things get a little less obvious.
Should node_modules be ignored? What about build output, environment files, IDE settings, caches, or framework-specific directories?
You can write the file yourself, copy one from another project, or search GitHub for an existing template.
I wanted to make that process a little easier, so I built DotGitIgnore.com.
DotGitIgnore is a free .gitignore generator for developers.
The idea is simple: choose the technologies, languages, frameworks, or tools you're using, and generate a .gitignore file that you can use in your project.
Instead of starting from an empty file or digging through repositories to find the right template, you can put together the rules you need in one place.
You can explore the available templates and build a file suited to your project without having to remember every generated directory or temporary file for every technology you use.
It's a small tool, but it's meant to solve a real problem that comes up during everyday development.
The basic interface for a tool like this is relatively straightforward.
The more interesting challenge is the template collection behind it.
Different languages and frameworks have different conventions. Even within the same ecosystem, the files you want Git to ignore can vary depending on your workflow.
A template that works well for one project might not be enough for another. And blindly combining every possible ignore rule would make the output unnecessarily large and difficult to understand.

title: Let the LLM Talk, Let a Script Do the Math: A Three-Part Pattern for Decision Agents
summary: Architectural pattern that separates AI reasoning from deterministic computation—letting LLMs interpret user intent while local scripts handle optimization and math—improves speed, cost, and accuracy for decision-making problems like coupon matching.
content:
A quick test


You have two McDonald's coupons and can use only one:
Spend 40, get 10 off
12% off any burger
You order a ¥25 burger:
Threshold coupon: you'd have to add ¥15 more → pay ¥30
Percentage coupon: 25 × 0.88 = ¥22 → the percentage coupon wins



Now make that burger ¥40:
Threshold coupon: pay ¥30 → the threshold coupon wins

Percentage coupon: pay ¥35.2
Which coupon is cheaper depends entirely on what's in the order. There is no general answer.
That's two coupons and one item. A real order is three coupons, twenty items, plus constraints like "two people, under ¥50, keep it under 1100 kcal, at least 35g protein." The number of combinations that satisfy all of that runs into the thousands.
Ask an LLM to solve that and you get three predictable outcomes:
Slow — thousands of multiply-adds, generated token by token
Expensive — every step burns tokens
Wrong — LLM arithmetic, as anyone who's tried it knows
So this project started from one rule:
The LLM handles understanding and expression. A script handles computation and determinism.
User speaks plainly
   │  "two people, under ¥50, nothing too greasy"
   ▼
LLM (WorkBuddy) parses intent ──► hard constraints
   │  max_payable=45, max_calories=1100, min_protein=35
   ▼
McDonald's MCP fetches real data ──► store menu / nutrition / coupons
   │
   ▼
optimize_meal.py (local, no network) ──► enumerate + best-coupon match
   │
   ▼
LLM turns results back into plain language ──► three plans




Role
Owns
Doesn't own




LLM
Interpreting "nothing too greasy"; narrating results
Money math, calorie math, remembering menus


MCP
Structured, trustworthy data
Decisions


Local script
Enumeration, filtering, coupon matching, ranking
Natural language



The payoff is direct: the script runs in milliseconds, is reproducible, costs zero tokens, and never gets the money wrong.

title: RethinkDB at 1,419 Matches and Nothing on 28015: When the Driver Port Is the Right Question
summary: Analysis using ZoomEye search data illustrates how product counts and port scans reveal different aspects of RethinkDB deployment exposure, demonstrating that port-level queries show whether services are published to the internet.
content:
RethinkDB at 1,419 Matches and Nothing on 28015: When the Driver Port Is the Right Question


A measurement that returns zero is often the most informative result in a set, provided the query behind it was the right one. The RethinkDB pair shows both halves of that statement.
Both queries ran on 2026-10-02 in the all-types scope.
app="RethinkDB", returned 1,419 matches.
https://www.zoomeye.ai/searchResult?q=YXBwPSJSZXRoaW5rREIi
port=28015, returned zero matches.
https://www.zoomeye.ai/searchResult?q=cG9ydD0yODAxNQ%3D%3D
A zero is a claim about the world, and it is only as strong as the query. A query for a port with no other condition is a weak instrument: it counts whatever happened to answer on that port and be recorded, and it says nothing about which software is listening.
A web administration console is a different interface with different rules. It presents a UI, it is frequently placed behind a proxy, and it exposes a JSON endpoint alongside the pages.
The first question is which addresses the cluster interfaces are bound to. A cluster that binds its driver, its intra-cluster port and its console to private interfaces has no external exposure regardless of the software's own authentication behaviour.
The pair illustrates a general point about exposure measurement. A product count answers whether something is installed. A port count answers whether a particular interface is published. Neither answers whether the interface is reachable to an authenticated user, and the zero here is only meaningful because the port in question is one that sensible deployments do not publish.
[1] ZoomEye search, app="RethinkDB", executed 2026-10-02 UTC, exact total 1,419. https://www.zoomeye.ai/searchResult?q=YXBwPSJSZXRoaW5rREIi

[2] ZoomEye search, port=28015, executed 2026-10-02 UTC, exact total 0. https://www.zoomeye.ai/searchResult?q=cG9ydD0yODAxNQ%3D%3D

[3] RethinkDB project home page. https://rethinkdb.com/

Agent Reasoning
      ↓
Policy / Authorization
      ↓
Financial Services
      ↓
Payment Rail

The important architectural question is no longer only:
Who authenticated?
It also becomes:
What exactly is software acting on behalf of that customer allowed to do?
An AI agent can interpret ambiguous instructions, gather information, choose tools, retry operations, and coordinate multiple services.
That flexibility is useful.
But financial systems cannot allow probabilistic reasoning to become the final source of authority.
Consider a customer instruction:
Pay my broadband bill every month if it stays below ₹1,500.
This is not a direct payment command.
It contains several constraints that first need to become structured financial intent:
{
  "intentType": "PAY_BILL",
  "billerId": "ISP_291",
  "maximumAmountMinor": 150000,
  "currency": "INR"
}

The agent can help interpret the instruction.
But the payment system should execute the structured contract—not the original natural-language sentence.
That boundary creates a useful architectural rule:
Reasoning may be probabilistic. Financial execution should remain deterministic.
A customer may successfully authenticate, but that does not mean an agent should automatically receive every permission available to the customer.
Instead of handing the agent broad account authority, the platform can create a bounded delegation:
action: PAY_BILL
biller: ISP_291
maxAmount: 150000
expiresAt: ...

The exact implementation might use scopes, server-side grants, capability tokens, mandates, or another authorization model.
The principle is the same:
Give the agent only the authority req

title: I Shipped 8 Free AI Writing Tools With Zero Budget — Here's What I Learned
summary: Developer built eight free writing tools with zero API costs by using deterministic algorithms instead of LLMs, removing signup barriers, and processing text client-side for privacy, finding 90% of real usage doesn't require neural networks.
content:
People keep asking me how much I'm paying in API bills. The answer is zero. Not "free tier" zero — actually zero.
Earlier this year I launched HumanWritr (https://humanwritr.com/), eight writing tools: a text humanizer, paraphraser, grammar checker, AI detector, plagiarism checker, word counter, AI SEO content writer, and an AI image detector. No funding, no team, no LLM API. Just me, a Cloudflare Worker, and an unreasonable amount of coffee.
Here's what I figured out along the way.
This was the big realization. Everyone assumes "AI writing tool" means piping everything through GPT. But think about what users actually do: fix grammar, reword a paragraph, count words, check if text looks AI-generated.
A paraphraser with a serious synonym database handles rewording fine. Grammar rules catch grammar errors — that's literally what they're for. An AI detector looking at linguistic markers (sentence uniformity, predictable word choices) does the job without a neural network. These deterministic approaches are instant, they cost nothing per request, and they work offline.
Sure, they won't write you a novel. But 90% of real usage isn't "write me a novel." It's "fix this paragraph."
I didn't plan this as a feature. Running everything client-side was originally just a cost decision — no servers processing text means no server bills. But then users started mentioning it in feedback: they liked that their drafts never left their browser.
Think about it — people paste cover letters, business plans, personal essays into these tools. "We don't see your text because we can't see your text" is a stronger privacy promise than any policy page. Architecture as a feature. I'll take it.
Every signup form is a tiny rejection. "Give me your email before I'll help you." I removed the requirement completely — every tool works the second the page loads. There's a login if you want it. Nothing needs it.
I can't give you exact numbers, but the difference in usage before and after was not subtle
